feature.1.tier_reason: Core: nearly every profile opens this way.
feature.1.why: A news lead tells readers who this is; an opening frame lets them see first. A moment, an action, makes readers ask their own question: what is he waiting for? Curiosity is lit before information arrives, so the background that follows has someone willing to read it.
feature.1.example: > *Demonstration:* At 4:20 a.m., Old Zhou lifted the third pot of soy milk off the stove and glanced at the clock on the wall. For nineteen years he has woken before the alarm in this breakfast shop.
feature.1.breakdown:
- “4:20 a.m.”: an exact time that can be pinned down.
- “The third pot”: one number hints at how long he has been at it.
- “Glanced at the clock”: action in place of thought.
- “Nineteen years”: the time variable is planted by the second sentence.
feature.1.overdo:
> It was a bright and sunny morning, the air filled with the scent of hope, and an ordinary yet great soul was about to awaken.

The fault: the picture is a filter, not a scene; “great” is outright lyricism; not one detail can be checked.
feature.1.when_not:
- When you didn't witness the moment or get it from reliable interviews; never invent a frame.
- Pure policy explainers, where readers want information, not a scene.
feature.1.exercise: Write a two-sentence opening frame for someone you know. It must contain an exact time and an action.
feature.1.check: Does the first paragraph contain “was born in” or “graduated from”? If so, it is not an opening frame.
feature.1.adjacent:
- feature.6: the contrast claim, the other opening hook, using a judgment instead of a picture.
- feature.2: the epigraph, placed before the opening frame, sets the tone rather than entering the scene.

feature.2.tier_reason: Signature: a recognisable device of this feature style, used sparingly.
feature.2.why: A public-domain literary line hands readers a key first, so the person who follows is read inside a larger theme. It explains nothing; it quietly sets the way of reading. When readers finish the profile and look back, they find the two lock together.
feature.2.example:
> *Demonstration:* Epigraph: “The starlight we see may have left its star tens of thousands of years ago.” (Invented line, not a quotation.)
>
> The text turns: She worked the night shift at the observatory for thirty years and, on the day she retired, did not take a single star chart with her.
feature.2.breakdown:
- The epigraph is only about light arriving late; it doesn't mention the person.
- The person and the “thirty years” appear only in the first line of the text.
- “Did not take a single star chart” quietly echoes the lateness in the epigraph, without pointing it out.
feature.2.overdo:
> Epigraph: “Life is a journey; what matters is not the destination but the scenery along the way.”

The fault: a feel-good line with no source and no fit with the person; pure decoration.
feature.2.when_not:
- When the quotation doesn't match the person's situation.
- When you aren't sure of the source. Never invent words for a famous writer; better to use none.
feature.2.exercise: Choose a public-domain classical poem line as an epigraph for the person from the feature.1 exercise, and write one sentence (not for the text) on where it locks with them.
feature.2.check: Remove the epigraph: is the text completely unaffected? If so, it doesn't lock.
feature.2.adjacent:
- feature.9: section titles use the same restrained poetry, but to divide sections.
- feature.1: the opening frame.

feature.3.tier_reason: Core: quotes carry most of the feeling in any profile.
feature.3.why: Readers are on guard against a reporter's descriptions, not against what the subject says in their own words. One short, spoken line sounds more like the truth than a paragraph of paraphrase; add a physical detail like “paused for a moment” and readers can see the instant it was said.
feature.3.example: > *Demonstration:* Asked whether she had regrets, she folded the rag in her hands twice and said, “What good's regretting. Work.”
feature.3.breakdown:
- “Folded the rag twice”: a physical detail that speaks for her hesitation.
- “What good's regretting.”: very short, colloquial.
- “Work.”: one word puts the attitude into action.
- The reporter adds no judgment.
feature.3.overdo:
> She said with deep feeling, “I think the most important thing in life is to hold on to your dreams, never give up, and be grateful for everyone you meet.”

The fault: the quote is written-sounding and inspirational, as if polished; “with deep feeling” is the reporter emoting.
feature.3.when_not:
- When the subject's words aren't suitable, choose another line or none. Never rewrite or polish.
- Words touching on privacy, or that could harm the subject.
feature.3.exercise: Interview someone near you about “the most tiring day”. Pick one verbatim line of 15 characters or fewer and write it with one physical detail.
feature.3.check: Is the quote unaltered, word for word? Is it 15 characters or fewer?
feature.3.adjacent:
- feature.8: restrained feeling, for which quotes are the main vehicle.
- feature.4: situated detail, the source of the physical detail.

feature.4.tier_reason: Core: the factual texture of every profile depends on it.
feature.4.why: A good detail can state the job, the years and the cost all at once, carrying three more layers than an adjective. Because it serves the situation, readers don't find it voyeuristic. Because it has a source, readers can trust it.
feature.4.example: > *Demonstration:* After twenty years of repairing watches, his right eye spends more time squinting than open. When he had his ID photo taken, the photographer asked for “both eyes the same size”. He tried three times. (Source: the subject's own account.)
feature.4.breakdown:
- “Right eye squinting”: a work gesture settled into the body.
- “Tried three times”: the detail brings out the cost without saying “hard work”.
- The bracketed source answers “how do you know?”
feature.4.overdo:
> His office was full of trophies, books, plants, coffee cups and a family photo, and outside a light rain was falling.

The fault: details piled up with no bearing on the situation; the “light rain”, without a source, is invention.
feature.4.when_not:
- When a detail can't answer “how do you know?”, cut it.
- When a detail is merely curious and unrelated to the person's situation.
feature.4.exercise: Watch a worker's hands or tools and write one detail that shows how long they have done the job, with its source.
feature.4.check: Can every detail say which it came from: interview, observation or documents?
feature.4.adjacent:
- feature.3: quotes carry the load, with physical detail set beside the quote.
- feature.1: the opening frame often uses one situated detail.

feature.5.tier_reason: Common: used whenever a long life must be covered in little space.
feature.5.why: With years and ages packed close together, readers see in seconds a person pushed along by time; the coolness of a CV makes the change weigh more. It also frees space for the parts the piece will open up.
feature.5.example: > *Demonstration:* At 14 she joined the county troupe to learn the banhu; at 19 she toured the countryside with it; at 31 the troupe disbanded and she went to a textile mill as a loom operator; at 52 she retired and took the banhu out from under the bed again.
feature.5.breakdown:
- Four ages as time markers, so each change can be placed.
- Plain verbs: joined, toured, disbanded, took out.
- The last action returns to her old craft, leaving room for the change the piece will write about.
feature.5.overdo:
> Her life went through countless storms and also gained countless rainbows; every experience made her stronger.

The fault: not one year or event. This is abstract summary, not compression.
feature.5.when_not:
- When the life story is flat and has nothing to do with the change in situation.
- For a famous person whose biography readers already know; compressing it is just repetition.
feature.5.exercise: Write a one-paragraph biography of an older relative using four age points, in no more than 70 characters.
feature.5.check: Are there at least three years or ages in the paragraph? Any adjectives?
feature.5.adjacent:
- feature.9: section titles cut time into blocks; compressed biography covers it in one paragraph.
- feature.1: the opening frame.

feature.6.tier_reason: Common: a frequent opening hook when the subject has a real anomaly.
feature.6.why: When readers see something that shouldn't be, they instinctively want to know why. The claim is the question the whole piece answers, giving loose material a thematic hook. It only states the contrast; it doesn't judge right or wrong.
feature.6.example: > *Demonstration:* In a village where everyone wants to move to the city, he is one of the few who moved back from it, and he means to stay.
feature.6.breakdown:
- “Everyone wants to move to the city”: first set the norm.
- “Moved back from it”: the point of contrast.
- “Means to stay”: extends the contrast into the future, which the piece must explain.
feature.6.overdo:
> He is an extraordinary ordinary man, writing an extraordinary legend of life through ordinary perseverance.

The fault: “extraordinary” is an empty claim with no verifiable contrast, and it reads like propaganda.
feature.6.when_not:
- For a purely private person with no public issue behind them, the contrast tends to fall flat (the engine flags this as a blind spot).
- When the contrast is your guess rather than confirmed by reporting.
feature.6.exercise: Write a contrast claim about someone you know, in the form: “In a … where …, he/she is …”.
feature.6.check: Does the claim contain a norm that facts can prove and a departure from it?
feature.6.adjacent: - feature.1: the opening frame opens with a picture; the two can follow each other.

feature.7.tier_reason: Signature: the method for event-driven group stories, used only in that kind of piece.
feature.7.why: Numbers numb people; specific individuals don't. Each slice is short, yet readers feel the weight accumulating. The weight comes from number piled on specificity, not from description.
feature.7.example: > *Demonstration:* (Fictional event.) On that night bus, in the third row sat a retired teacher going to the provincial capital for a follow-up check, a sweater her husband had half knitted in her bag; in the back row was a young man who had just got his licence, his first road-trip route saved on his phone.
feature.7.breakdown:
- Each person gets a seat, an identity and one thing they carried.
- The objects (sweater, route map) carry unfinished lives.
- No adjectives about the outcome; the slices just sit side by side.
feature.7.overdo:
> Among them were old people, children and young people; each one was the whole of a family, which is unbearably heartbreaking.

The fault: only categories, no specific people, and it ends in open lyricism.
feature.7.when_not:
- When you can't verify each individual's information; better to write fewer people.
- When the families haven't agreed to disclosure.
feature.7.exercise: Invent a small scene (a classroom, say) and write three slices of no more than 30 characters each, each with one object.
feature.7.check: Can each slice stand on its own? Is there any lyrical adjective in the passage?
feature.7.adjacent:
- feature.8: restrained feeling, which group stories must pair with.
- feature.4: situated detail.

feature.8.tier_reason: Core: the baseline tone of the whole genre, with almost no exceptions.
feature.8.why: Told “grief-stricken”, readers receive one word; shown the facts, they produce the feeling themselves, and feeling they produce goes deeper. Restraint is also where features naturally resist AI-sounding prose.
feature.8.example: > *Demonstration:* After her daughter died, she still cooked for two every day. The second portion went into the fridge, and the next day at noon she heated it up and ate it herself.
feature.8.breakdown:
- “Cooked for two”: one fact carries the whole loss.
- “Heated it up and ate it herself”: life goes on, the pain hidden in the action.
- Not one emotion word in the passage.
feature.8.overdo:
> At that moment, tears streamed down her face, she was overcome with grief, and everyone present was deeply moved.

The fault: three lyrical phrases in a row; the reporter is crying for the reader.
feature.8.when_not: - In features this has almost no exceptions; the only latitude is that emotion words the subject says in a quote may stay.
feature.8.exercise: Rewrite “he missed his hometown very much” as a single fact, with no emotion words.
feature.8.check: Search the text for “grief-stricken / great / shocking / tear-jerking / touching / inspiring”: zero hits?
feature.8.adjacent:
- feature.3: quotes carry the load.
- feature.7: ensemble slices.

feature.9.tier_reason: Common: used in any feature long enough to be divided into sections.
feature.9.why: Sections cut time into thematic blocks and give readers a breather and a direction. A noun phrase offers an image, not a conclusion, keeping suspense and letting each block run chronologically inside. Titles taken from objects in the text mean readers meet them again: they see “Right Eye” in a title, and a few paragraphs later read him squinting it to repair a watch; the image lands, and the title turns into a detail planted early. A noun has no predicate, so it doesn't judge “what he is like” for the reader; that is left to the facts in the text, in keeping with the feature principle that the reporter disappears. Read in a row, the titles form a minimal timeline.
feature.9.example: > *Demonstration:* A profile of a watch repairer, in three sections: “Mainspring”, “Right Eye”, “The Year It Stopped”.
feature.9.breakdown:
- All nouns or noun phrases, not sentences; no evaluative verbs like “persevering” or “guarding”.
- Each comes from a real object or detail in the text: “Mainspring” is a tool, “Right Eye” is the body, and both have matching passages.
- “The Year It Stopped” hints at change without saying what; readers must finish the section to learn whether it was the watch, the factory or the man that stopped.
- From object to person to time, the three tighten in turn, and the order itself has rhythm.
feature.9.overdo:
> Chapter One: “He Interprets the Craftsman Spirit Through Perseverance”

The fault: a complete judgment sentence that gives the game away and draws the conclusion.
feature.9.when_not:
- Pieces shorter than about 2,000 characters, where sections only interrupt.
- Group event stories told in time order, where timestamps can replace titles.
feature.9.exercise: Draft three noun section titles for a feature about a courier.
feature.9.check: Does any title have a verb predicate or a conclusion? If so, turn it into a noun.
feature.9.adjacent:
- feature.5: compressed biography.
- feature.2: the epigraph, the same restrained poetry in a different position.

feature.10.tier_reason: Common: standard for investigative features, unnecessary for pure profiles.
feature.10.why: The text keeps the story flowing and readers aren't interrupted by jargon; the list at the end gives readers who want to dig a path, and gives structural claims a basis that can be checked.
feature.10.example:
> *Demonstration:* Text: “He had worked it out: every extra junction on a delivery costs two more minutes. In a study of delivery routes, this has another name.”
>
> End: References (listing author, title, publication and year for what was actually cited).
feature.10.breakdown:
- “He had worked it out” connects the research to the person's experience.
- “Has another name”: mentions the research without dropping the term.
- The list includes only works actually read and cited.
feature.10.overdo:
> According to Maslow's hierarchy of needs and Foucault's theory of discipline, the alienation of food-delivery riders is significant.

The fault: the text is stacked with terms, the person vanishes, and it becomes a paper.
feature.10.when_not:
- Pure profiles with no structural argument.
- When sources haven't been verified; never list or invent them.
feature.10.exercise: Rewrite a jargon sentence (such as “information asymmetry”) as a detail of something that happened to a person.
feature.10.check: Has every academic concept in the text been turned into a person's experience? Can every item on the list be traced to the original?
feature.10.adjacent: - feature.4: situated detail; relaying research uses detail the same way.
